table.text: In both cases, after this initial encoding phase, all objects were tested in a subsequent old/new memory test to ensure they were memorized accurately regardless of block; finally, participants were asked to search for these objects in the hybrid visual search task.
table.header: Experiment 1: Hybrid search is better for more deeply encoded target sets

table.text: A further 16 participants were run and excluded based on the following criteria, chosen in advance: having an overall memory accuracy ≤ 50%, responding outside a 150-10,000 ms window on more than 10% of search trials, or having average search accuracy below 50%.
All procedures were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and participants provided informed consent.
In the encoding stage, participants were shown a set of items that needed to be memorized and subsequently searched for in that block.
Participants were given 1 question per trial and asked to type in a response to the question.
In the memory test stage, participants were tested on the items they had studied initially.

Test phase: Participants completed a recognition memory test where they judged whether each presented object was "old" (from the memorized set) or "new" (foil), followed by confidence ratings on a 1-6 scale.

Restricting target-present trials to targets each participant had correctly endorsed as "old" in the memory test, the encoding effect remained clearly significant in accuracy, F(1,74) = 16.12, p < .001, ηp² = .179, was attenuated in IES, F(1,74) = 3.96, p = .050, ηp² = .051, and was absent in RT (F(1,74) < 0.01, p = .994), as in the full data.

table.text: We recruited self-reported NFL and NHL fans, taking advantage of participants' strong pre-existing knowledge about sports logos.
table.header: Experiment 2: Inverting the memory set-size effect

table.text: Our final sample comprised 79 participants (mean age = 36.1 years, range 20-74; 63 male, 16 female) recruited via Prolific, where we could pre-screen their sports knowledge to selectively recruit NFL and NHL experts. 26 additional participants were tested and excluded for: any condition cell with an infinite inverse efficiency score, overall search accuracy below 50%, more than 10% of search responses outside the 500-4,500 ms window, or reporting interest in their nominally unfamiliar sport one or more scale points above their nominally familiar sport.
Participants were limited to be U.S. or Canadian-based and compensated at an hourly rate consistent with institutional guidelines.
All procedures were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and participants provided informed consent.

Participants were assigned to their experimental group -familiar with the NFL or familiar with the NHL -based on their reported familiarity for each league prior to the beginning of the study, using a Prolific pre-screen that allows selecting participants based on their sports' preferences.
In the study phase at the start of each block, participants were instructed to memorize the targets for that memory set.
After each response, participants were asked to rate their confidence in their answer on a scale from 1 to 6.
In the hybrid search stage of the experiment, for each block, participants completed 128 trials of visual search (Figure 3).
table.formatted: In the hybrid search stage of the experiment, for each block, participants completed 128 trials of visual search (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

table.text: Participants were instructed to indicate whether any target was present or absent in that trial by pressing "J" or "F" on their keyboard, respectively, while being as quick and accurate as possible.
After completing all trials in the first block, participants were encouraged to take a break if needed before moving onto the next block.

Previous literature has demonstrated that search performance can vary depending on whether participants are searching for any objects from a category or a specific target within a category (Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014).

In the search stage, for each block, participants completed 128 trials of visual search (Figure 5).

Lure costs did not differ significantly between familiar and unfamiliar blocks (interactions: accuracy F(1,74) = 0.45, p = .504, ηp² = .006; RT F(1,73) = 3.26, p = .075, ηp² = .043), so participants are not doing categorical search in their preferred sport.

At the same time, lure-present target-absent displays were correctly rejected on 87% of trials, so participants were easily discriminating studied from unstudied logos rather than merely detecting the relevant category.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Sample sizes for all experiments were set in advance at approximately 75 participants after exclusions, providing >95% power to detect within-subject effects of dz ≥ 0.45 at α = .05, and exceeding typical samples in hybrid search studies (e.g., Wolfe, 2012).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 75, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.95, effect_size = 0.45, effect_size_metric = "Cohen's d", software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "Sample sizes for all experiments were set in advance at approximately 75 participants after exclusions, providing >95% power to detect within-subject effects of dz ≥ 0.45 at α = .05, and exceeding typical samples in hybrid search studies (e.g., Wolfe, 2012)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 1 t-test and/or F-test where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: Memory was reliably stronger in the deepencoding block, d′ = 4.33 (SD = 0.59), than in the shallow-encoding block, d′ = 3.27 (SD = 1.05), t(74) = 8.27, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.95 (hits: .97 vs. .85; false alarms: .02 vs. .05).

Note that, consistent with global matching models, but not straightforwardly consistent with a search process, the stronger list led to fewer false alarms t(74) = 4.20, p < .001, dz = 0.49), a 'mirror effect' whereby strong memories make you better able to reject new items, not just better at recognizing old items (Criss, 2006; Stretch & Wixted, 1998).

live_data_statements: In another block, each item was shown 8 times and each time it was seen, participants had to give a short response related to the item to increase memory strength (deep-encoding block).

In both cases, after this initial encoding phase, all objects were tested in a subsequent old/new memory test to ensure they were memorized accurately regardless of block; finally, participants were asked to search for these objects in the hybrid visual search task.

A further 16 participants were run and excluded based on the following criteria, chosen in advance: having an overall memory accuracy ≤ 50%, responding outside a 150-10,000 ms window on more than 10% of search trials, or having average search accuracy below 50%.
All procedures were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and participants provided informed consent.
In the encoding stage, participants were shown a set of items that needed to be memorized and subsequently searched for in that block.
Participants were given 1 question per trial and asked to type in a response to the question.
In the memory test stage, participants were tested on the items they had studied initially.

Test phase: Participants completed a recognition memory test where they judged whether each presented object was "old" (from the memorized set) or "new" (foil), followed by confidence ratings on a 1-6 scale.

Restricting target-present trials to targets each participant had correctly endorsed as "old" in the memory test, the encoding effect remained clearly significant in accuracy, F(1,74) = 16.12, p < .001, ηp² = .179, was attenuated in IES, F(1,74) = 3.96, p = .050, ηp² = .051, and was absent in RT (F(1,74) < 0.01, p = .994), as in the full data.
We recruited self-reported NFL and NHL fans, taking advantage of participants' strong pre-existing knowledge about sports logos.

Our final sample comprised 79 participants (mean age = 36.1 years, range 20-74; 63 male, 16 female) recruited via Prolific, where we could pre-screen their sports knowledge to selectively recruit NFL and NHL experts. 26 additional participants were tested and excluded for: any condition cell with an infinite inverse efficiency score, overall search accuracy below 50%, more than 10% of search responses outside the 500-4,500 ms window, or reporting interest in their nominally unfamiliar sport one or more scale points above their nominally familiar sport.
Participants were limited to be U.S. or Canadian-based and compensated at an hourly rate consistent with institutional guidelines.

Participants were assigned to their experimental group -familiar with the NFL or familiar with the NHL -based on their reported familiarity for each league prior to the beginning of the study, using a Prolific pre-screen that allows selecting participants based on their sports' preferences.
In the study phase at the start of each block, participants were instructed to memorize the targets for that memory set.
After each response, participants were asked to rate their confidence in their answer on a scale from 1 to 6.
In the hybrid search stage of the experiment, for each block, participants completed 128 trials of visual search (Figure 3).
Participants were instructed to indicate whether any target was present or absent in that trial by pressing "J" or "F" on their keyboard, respectively, while being as quick and accurate as possible.
After completing all trials in the first block, participants were encouraged to take a break if needed before moving onto the next block.

Previous literature has demonstrated that search performance can vary depending on whether participants are searching for any objects from a category or a specific target within a category (Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014).

The final sample included 75 participants (mean age = 36.7 years, range 19-72; 48 male, 26 female, 1 other/undisclosed) recruited via Prolific based on the self-reported sports familiarity. 38 additional participants were run and excluded using the same criteria as above.
In the search stage, for each block, participants completed 128 trials of visual search (Figure 5).

Lure costs did not differ significantly between familiar and unfamiliar blocks (interactions: accuracy F(1,74) = 0.45, p = .504, ηp² = .006; RT F(1,73) = 3.26, p = .075, ηp² = .043), so participants are not doing categorical search in their preferred sport.

At the same time, lure-present target-absent displays were correctly rejected on 87% of trials, so participants were easily discriminating studied from unstudied logos rather than merely detecting the relevant category.

text.text: In hybrid search tasks, observers search for any of multiple targets held in memory (e.g., finding all of the ingredients for a recipe in the supermarket).
Performance declines with the log of the number of memorized targets, a cost often attributed to a serial scan through memory.

In standard models of recognition memory, however, holding more items in memory weakens the match strength between each memory representation and the corresponding visual itemindependent of any serial search process.
Here we propose an account of hybrid search based on memory strength, testing how memory strength affects hybrid search separately from memory set size.
We found that strengthening memories through repetition and deeper encoding improved hybrid search at matched set sizes (Exp.

Taking advantage of NFL and NHL fans' pre-existing memory strength for sports logos (Exps. 2-3), we next found search was better for a larger set of familiar items (16 logos) than for a smaller set of unfamiliar items (12 logos), a reversal of the usual memory set-size effect.

A standard global matching model (REM), with encoding parameters fit only to memory performance, not search data, reproduced these results and the canonical, approximately log-linear set-size cost in discriminability.
Memory strength is thus a potentially strong determinant of hybrid search efficiency, with set-size effects not necessarily reflecting any serial memory search.
Instead, models of recognition memory may provide a productive framework for the memory component of hybrid search.
We perform visual search tasks many times a day, from rifling through a bag to find our keys, to looking for a familiar face in a crowded room.
Often we search not for a single object but with many potential targets in mind, a task known as hybrid search (Wolfe, 2012).
text.formatted: Often we search not for a single object but with many potential targets in mind, a task known as hybrid search <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wolfe, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For example, we might look for any member of our friend group in a crowd, or for all the ingredients of a recipe at the supermarket.
For some people, hybrid search is a core aspect of their occupation, as when airport security officers screen luggage for many kinds of potential hazards.
People take for granted how easy such searches usually are.
Within a few seconds we either find a friend in a crowd or conclude they are not there and move on to search elsewhere.
In the current work, we test the role of memory strength in hybrid search.

We ask whether how strongly the to-be-searched-for items are represented in memory shapes performance, above and beyond the pure number of items being searched for, which has so far been the factor that has dominated most theorizing about these tasks.

Previous work has shown that the time to complete a hybrid search increases linearly with the number of items in the visual display and logarithmically with the number of items in the memory set (Wolfe, 2012).
text.formatted: Previous work has shown that the time to complete a hybrid search increases linearly with the number of items in the visual display and logarithmically with the number of items in the memory set <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wolfe, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These linear and logarithmic relationships hold across stimulus types, including alphanumeric characters, objects, words, and categories (Boettcher & Wolfe, 2015; Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014).
text.formatted: These linear and logarithmic relationships hold across stimulus types, including alphanumeric characters, objects, words, and categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Boettcher & Wolfe, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: They extend to temporal (RSVP) search (Drew & Wolfe, 2014) and persist when the number of memorized items far exceeds working memory limits (Wolfe, 2012), suggesting that the searched target sets are held in activated long-term memory rather than solely working memory (Drew et al., 2016).
text.formatted: They extend to temporal (RSVP) search <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Drew & Wolfe, 2014)</ref> and persist when the number of memorized items far exceeds working memory limits <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wolfe, 2012)</ref>, suggesting that the searched target sets are held in activated long-term memory rather than solely working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Drew et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers generally treat these regularities as reflecting the core processes at work in hybrid search (e.g., Wolfe, 2012).
text.formatted: Researchers generally treat these regularities as reflecting the core processes at work in hybrid search (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Although memory search consistently behaves differently from visual search, in the hybrid search literature, both are generally conceived of as fundamentally search processes, that is, as some process of 'looking through' a collection of discrete items.

Indeed, the initial prediction of Wolfe (2012) was that memory set size, like visual set size, would produce linear costs; the logarithmic result instead motivated the proposal that memory is searched with an efficient, logarithmic-search-like algorithm, producing "the pattern that would be seen if half the items could be eliminated on the first step, another half on the next step, and so on" (Wolfe, 2012), so that an N-item list requires only log₂(N) comparisons.
text.formatted: Indeed, the initial prediction of <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe (2012)</ref> was that memory set size, like visual set size, would produce linear costs; the logarithmic result instead motivated the proposal that memory is searched with an efficient, logarithmic-search-like algorithm, producing "the pattern that would be seen if half the items could be eliminated on the first step, another half on the next step, and so on" <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wolfe, 2012)</ref>, so that an N-item list requires only log₂(N) comparisons.

text.text: Hybrid search performance, according to this view, is primarily driven by the number of items in both the visual and memory sets, an understanding that has largely remained dominant in subsequent work, sometimes explicitly and often implicitly (Boettcher et al., 2018; Drew et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Hybrid search performance, according to this view, is primarily driven by the number of items in both the visual and memory sets, an understanding that has largely remained dominant in subsequent work, sometimes explicitly and often implicitly <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Boettcher et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Drew et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The search-through-discrete-items metaphor is relatively well grounded in the case of visual search, although simple serial accounts have repeatedly given way to more graded ones that nonetheless treat display items as discrete, individually inspectable objects.

For example, while models of visual search have often combined parallel "guidance" of attention by target features with capacity-limited identification stages (Wolfe, 2007 (Wolfe, , 2020;; Wolfe & Horowitz, 2017); other models in this literature do derive set-size costs, including logarithmic RT functions, from solely parallel evidence accumulation (Lleras et al., 2020), with efficiency governed by the similarity structure of the underlying representations (Chapman & Störmer, 2024).
text.formatted: For example, while models of visual search have often combined parallel "guidance" of attention by target features with capacity-limited identification stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Wolfe, 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Wolfe, , 2020;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Wolfe & Horowitz, 2017)</ref>; other models in this literature do derive set-size costs, including logarithmic RT functions, from solely parallel evidence accumulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Lleras et al., 2020)</ref>, with efficiency governed by the similarity structure of the underlying representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chapman & Störmer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Formal model comparisons suggest that limited-capacity parallel processing may be sufficient for most search tasks (Thornton & Gilden, 2007), even as sophisticated serial models remain competitive on benchmark RT distributions (Moran et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Formal model comparisons suggest that limited-capacity parallel processing may be sufficient for most search tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Thornton & Gilden, 2007)</ref>, even as sophisticated serial models remain competitive on benchmark RT distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Moran et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while some component of serial processing is common in considering visual search processes (particularly given eye movements are necessarily serial), and objects on the search display are indeed discrete, separate entities in nearly all search task, even in this domain the architecture question has remained difficult to resolve (Townsend, 1990).
text.formatted: Thus, while some component of serial processing is common in considering visual search processes (particularly given eye movements are necessarily serial), and objects on the search display are indeed discrete, separate entities in nearly all search task, even in this domain the architecture question has remained difficult to resolve <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Townsend, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Our focus here is the other, less-commonlyexamined component of hybrid search: the memory decision made about each inspected item.
Hybrid search is necessarily a recognition memory task.
Indeed, at a visual set size of one item, it is exactly equivalent to a standard old/new recognition task.

Nevertheless, existing models of hybrid search have generally had little to say about the strength of the individual memory representations being searched, even though this is a core aspect of how recognition memory is modeled and conceived of.
This is at least partly by design rather than oversight.

In standard hybrid search paradigms, observers learn the memory set to a criterion precisely so that differences in memory quality can (hopefully) be set aside without major consequences (e.g., Wolfe, 2012; Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014).
text.formatted: In standard hybrid search paradigms, observers learn the memory set to a criterion precisely so that differences in memory quality can (hopefully) be set aside without major consequences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: But this methodological choice has had a theoretical consequence, since the resulting models treat memory-set items as interchangeable units, present on the list -and in memory -or not.
Treating items this way makes memory search more analogous to visual search, and likely contributed to proposals like the logarithmic search of Wolfe (2012).
text.formatted: Treating items this way makes memory search more analogous to visual search, and likely contributed to proposals like the logarithmic search of <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe (2012)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, this treatment contrasts strongly with how memory is conceived in the recognition memory literature, where models typically assume that performance is governed by graded match signals that vary with encoding quality, repetition, distinctiveness, and interference (Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997; Wixted, 2007), rather than reflecting a search through a discrete set of items.
text.formatted: Notably, this treatment contrasts strongly with how memory is conceived in the recognition memory literature, where models typically assume that performance is governed by graded match signals that vary with encoding quality, repetition, distinctiveness, and interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark & Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Wixted, 2007)</ref>, rather than reflecting a search through a discrete set of items.

text.text: Indeed, there are already hints in the hybrid search literature itself that item-level memory quality matters, even when participants study the list to a fixed accuracy criterion.

Search is markedly less efficient for categorically defined targets than for specific memorized pictures (Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014), the targets' value modulates their priority within a memory set (Wolfe et al., 2018), and in a dataset of roughly nine million hybrid search trials, item-level memorability measures strongly predict which targets were found and which distractors were rejected (Simpson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Search is markedly less efficient for categorically defined targets than for specific memorized pictures <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014)</ref>, the targets' value modulates their priority within a memory set <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Wolfe et al., 2018)</ref>, and in a dataset of roughly nine million hybrid search trials, item-level memorability measures strongly predict which targets were found and which distractors were rejected <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Simpson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Outside hybrid search, other work also suggests that the strength of memories modulates visual search.

For example, naturally familiar brand logos are found faster than unfamiliar ones in standard visual search, an advantage that brief laboratory training does not reproduce (Qin et al., 2014); long-term familiarity with distractors likewise makes them faster to reject (Wang et al., 1994).
text.formatted: For example, naturally familiar brand logos are found faster than unfamiliar ones in standard visual search, an advantage that brief laboratory training does not reproduce <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Qin et al., 2014)</ref>; long-term familiarity with distractors likewise makes them faster to reject <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Wang et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: What has been missing is a direct test of whether memory strength shapes hybrid search efficiency when the number of items in memory is held constant, or when the two are pitted against each other.

Furthermore, once the role of memory strength is acknowledged, it is important to test to what extent memory strength might explain the generally large effects of memory set size, as larger lists generally will be expected to produce weaker and more variable match signals -potentially allowing standard recognition models to explain some or even all of the memory set size effect.

The idea that memory is searched serially -as in Wolfe's logarithmic search proposal (2012) --originates with Sternberg's (1966 Sternberg's ( , 1969) ) memory-scanning experiments, in which response times to classify a probe as belonging to a small memorized set increased linearly with set size (~38 ms/item), with equal slopes for positive and negative probes.
text.formatted: The idea that memory is searched serially -as in Wolfe's logarithmic search proposal (2012) --originates with <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Sternberg's (1966</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Sternberg's ( , 1969) )</ref> memory-scanning experiments, in which response times to classify a probe as belonging to a small memorized set increased linearly with set size (~38 ms/item), with equal slopes for positive and negative probes.

text.text: Sternberg interpreted this as serial exhaustive scanning, in which every item is compared before any response, producing strictly linear set-size functions.
By contrast, self-terminating variants, which stop at a match, produce a mixture of fast and slow positive responses.
However, modern recognition memory models do not generally conceieve of recognition as a search process in this way.
This is because subsequent work undermined the serial-scanning interpretation on several fronts.

With larger, well-learned memory sets, RT grows with the logarithm of set size rather than linearly, which seems inconsistent with constant-time-per-comparison scanning (Burrows & Okada, 1975); this is the same functional form later observed in hybrid search (Wolfe, 2012).
text.formatted: With larger, well-learned memory sets, RT grows with the logarithm of set size rather than linearly, which seems inconsistent with constant-time-per-comparison scanning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burrows & Okada, 1975)</ref>; this is the same functional form later observed in hybrid search <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wolfe, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Proberecognition RTs show strong recency gradients consistent with direct, strength-based access rather than exhaustive comparison (Monsell, 1978).
text.formatted: Proberecognition RTs show strong recency gradients consistent with direct, strength-based access rather than exhaustive comparison <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Monsell, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: And when retrieval speed and retrieval success are separated with response-signal methods, set size appears to affect the amount of evidence available rather than the rate of access, as expected if all comparisons proceed in parallel (McElree & Dosher, 1989).
text.formatted: And when retrieval speed and retrieval success are separated with response-signal methods, set size appears to affect the amount of evidence available rather than the rate of access, as expected if all comparisons proceed in parallel <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(McElree & Dosher, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Formal modeling points to the same conclusion: parallel evidence-accumulation models reproduce Sternberg's linear functions without any serial scan (Ratcliff, 1978), and modern comparisons of serial, parallel, and global-access architectures against full RT distributions favor strength-based global access under the conditions that best discriminate the architectures (Donkin & Nosofsky, 2012; Nosofsky et al., 2011), though, as in visual search, the architectures mimic one another closely elsewhere.
text.formatted: Formal modeling points to the same conclusion: parallel evidence-accumulation models reproduce Sternberg's linear functions without any serial scan <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Ratcliff, 1978)</ref>, and modern comparisons of serial, parallel, and global-access architectures against full RT distributions favor strength-based global access under the conditions that best discriminate the architectures <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Donkin & Nosofsky, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Nosofsky et al., 2011)</ref>, though, as in visual search, the architectures mimic one another closely elsewhere.

text.text: In the recognition memory literature, then, the dominant framework that emerged from this history is the family of global matching models: for example, to name a few well known examples, SAM (Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984), MINERVA 2 (Hintzman, 1988), TODAM (Murdock, 1982), the Matrix model (Humphreys et al., 1989), and REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997; for reviews, Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Osth & Dennis, 2024).
text.formatted: In the recognition memory literature, then, the dominant framework that emerged from this history is the family of global matching models: for example, to name a few well known examples, SAM <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984)</ref>, MINERVA 2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hintzman, 1988)</ref>, TODAM <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Murdock, 1982)</ref>, the Matrix model <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Humphreys et al., 1989)</ref>, and REM <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997</ref>; for reviews, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Clark & Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Osth & Dennis, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These models share a simple premise: long-term memory stores a trace of every encoded item, and a recognition decision is made by comparing the probe in parallel against all stored traces, computing its summed similarity to them (or some close proxy).

The result is a single graded familiarity signal: high global similarity produces a confident "old" response ("I'm sure I've seen it"), and very low similarity produces a confident "new" response ("I'm sure I haven't seen it").
Critically, these models produce list-length costs without any serial search.

Each additional stored trace adds variance to the match signal, so discriminability declines as the variance of the strength distributions grows with list length (in the simplest summed-signal case, d′ ∝ 1/√N), a smooth decline that closely resembles a logarithmic function over typical ranges (Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Shiffrin et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Each additional stored trace adds variance to the match signal, so discriminability declines as the variance of the strength distributions grows with list length (in the simplest summed-signal case, d′ ∝ 1/√N), a smooth decline that closely resembles a logarithmic function over typical ranges <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark & Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Shiffrin et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Such models also explain -uniquely --why people can often rapidly and confidently reject novel items, because a low global match, or a diagnostic novel feature, supports an immediate "new" response without consulting each memory (Glucksberg & McCloskey, 1981; Osth et al., 2023), and highly familiar probes can be accepted on familiarity alone, without extended retrieval (Atkinson & Juola, 1974).
text.formatted: Such models also explain -uniquely --why people can often rapidly and confidently reject novel items, because a low global match, or a diagnostic novel feature, supports an immediate "new" response without consulting each memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Glucksberg & McCloskey, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Osth et al., 2023)</ref>, and highly familiar probes can be accepted on familiarity alone, without extended retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Atkinson & Juola, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: A simple serial search account, by contrast, would seem to require the entire set to be checked before rejecting, and so predicts target-absent decisions slower than target-present ones.

That prediction generally holds in the visual aspects of visual search, motivating the view of it as a search/accumulation process (Wolfe, 2020); in recognition memory, however, it often fails, suggesting that "search" analogies are a poor description of recognition memory, and motivating the global matching family of models instead.
text.formatted: That prediction generally holds in the visual aspects of visual search, motivating the view of it as a search/accumulation process <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Wolfe, 2020)</ref>; in recognition memory, however, it often fails, suggesting that "search" analogies are a poor description of recognition memory, and motivating the global matching family of models instead.

text.text: In particular, recognition reaction time data instead suggest that response speed tracks the strength of evidence for whichever response is made.

The fastest responses of all are typically high-confidence "old" decisions to strong targets (Murdock & Dufty, 1972), but strong "new" responses are also fast, and strengthening memory of a study list speeds the rejection of unstudied items as well as the acceptance of studied items (Criss, 2010; Hockley, 1982; Ratcliff & Murdock, 1976), unlike in visual search.
text.formatted: The fastest responses of all are typically high-confidence "old" decisions to strong targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Murdock & Dufty, 1972</ref>), but strong "new" responses are also fast, and strengthening memory of a study list speeds the rejection of unstudied items as well as the acceptance of studied items <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Criss, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hockley, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Ratcliff & Murdock, 1976)</ref>, unlike in visual search.

text.text: Formal models of these global matching frameworks can also explain reaction time effects like those observed in hybrid search.

For example, accumulation-based extensions of global matching models to response time, such as the exemplar-based random walk (EBRW; Nosofsky & Palmeri, 1997) and related accumulator models (Hockley & Murdock, 1987; Ratcliff, 1978), predict that longer lists produce slower as well as less accurate decisions, even at high accuracy.
text.formatted: For example, accumulation-based extensions of global matching models to response time, such as the exemplar-based random walk (EBRW; <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Nosofsky & Palmeri, 1997)</ref> and related accumulator models <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hockley & Murdock, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Ratcliff, 1978)</ref>, predict that longer lists produce slower as well as less accurate decisions, even at high accuracy.

text.text: Indeed, Nosofsky et al. (2014) showed that the curvilinear, approximately logarithmic RT functions that Wolfe (2012) attributed to logarithmic search arise naturally in an exemplar-familiarity model as memory set size increases from 1 to 16 in a standard old/new task.
text.formatted: Indeed, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nosofsky et al. (2014)</ref> showed that the curvilinear, approximately logarithmic RT functions that <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe (2012)</ref> attributed to logarithmic search arise naturally in an exemplar-familiarity model as memory set size increases from 1 to 16 in a standard old/new task.

text.text: Recognition memory models thus provide an alternative account of why hybrid search slows with memory set size: one with no "search" process at all, in which the operative variable is the strength of the match signal, and diagnostic signals lead to fast responses regardless of the number of items in memory.

As noted, a hybrid search display is, in effect, a recognition memory test with multiple simultaneous probes: each display item must be assessed as old (a target) or new (a distractor), much as eyewitness identification has recently been recast as a visual search task probing recognition memory (Wixted & Mickes, 2014; Wixted et al., 2021).
text.formatted: As noted, a hybrid search display is, in effect, a recognition memory test with multiple simultaneous probes: each display item must be assessed as old (a target) or new (a distractor), much as eyewitness identification has recently been recast as a visual search task probing recognition memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Wixted & Mickes, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wixted et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, hybrid search at a visual set size of one is a standard list-length manipulation of recognition memory, and is well captured by global matching models (Nosofsky et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Indeed, hybrid search at a visual set size of one is a standard list-length manipulation of recognition memory, and is well captured by global matching models <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Nosofsky et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: On this view of hybrid search as recognition memory, then, each item-decision in hybrid search is slower and less accurate with more items in memory not because more items must be serially examined, but because additional memories add noise that makes old and new items less discriminable.

This framing makes a distinctive prediction that list-based accounts do not: even among items encoded well enough to support near-ceiling recognition performance, variation in memory strength should modulate search efficiency -that is, items are not simply "on the list" or "not on the list".
This is because even for well-studied items, memory is not all-or-none.

Curvilinear ROCs in recognition suggest graded match strength even for well-learned items (Brady et al., 2023; Wixted, 2007), and strengthening encoding typically both raises hits and lowers false alarms (Criss, 2006; Stretch & Wixted, 1998) -not just making people more sure that items are on the list, but also faster and more accurate in rejecting items that are not on the list.
text.formatted: Curvilinear ROCs in recognition suggest graded match strength even for well-learned items <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brady et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Wixted, 2007)</ref>, and strengthening encoding typically both raises hits and lowers false alarms <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Criss, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Stretch & Wixted, 1998)</ref> -not just making people more sure that items are on the list, but also faster and more accurate in rejecting items that are not on the list.

text.text: In global matching models, deeper encoding stores more, and more accurate, features per item, making each item more discriminable from new items.

Such models therefore predict that improved memory strength should improve performance at a constant list length and, in reaction-time extended versions of global matching models, speed decisions as well.

For example, simulations using the global matching model REM at list lengths of 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 yield recognition d′ of approximately 2.2, 2.1, 1.7, 1.5, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, and 0.8, nearly log-linear in list length.

Doubling the feature-storage probability raises d′ to 3.5 at length 5 and 3.3 at length 10, and d′ remains above 2.0 even at length 1000.foot_0 Thus, in models like this, "list length" (memory set size) effects arise simply because the other items in memory add variance to the match signal, which lowers discriminability -not because of any search process.
text.formatted: Doubling the feature-storage probability raises d′ to 3.5 at length 5 and 3.3 at length 10, and d′ remains above 2.0 even at length 1000.<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> Thus, in models like this, "list length" (memory set size) effects arise simply because the other items in memory add variance to the match signal, which lowers discriminability -not because of any search process.

text.text: Thus, in such models any list length effect can be compensated for by increasing the strength of the underlying memories.
In the current work, we therefore tested whether memory strength shapes hybrid search efficiency independently of memory set size.

Throughout, we use memory strength to mean the discriminability of old from new items on a standard recognition test, e.g. how quickly and easily studied items can be told apart from new ones on the basis of their encoded features.

Experiment 1 manipulated strength directly at a fixed set size, as participants searched for two 32-item memory sets, one encoded once (as in standard hybrid search studies) and one encoded deeply through repetition and semantic elaboration (Craik, 2002; Craik & Tulving, 1975).
text.formatted: Experiment 1 manipulated strength directly at a fixed set size, as participants searched for two 32-item memory sets, one encoded once (as in standard hybrid search studies) and one encoded deeply through repetition and semantic elaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Craik, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Craik & Tulving, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: Experiments 2 and 3 pitted strength against set size, exploiting naturally occurring expertise: NFL and NHL fans memorized 16 logos from their familiar sport and 12 from the unfamiliar sport.

People tend to form richer, more distinctive memories for objects of expertise (Curby et al., 2009; Ericsson & Lehmann, 1996), so if strength dominates, search should be better for the larger, familiar set, reversing the memory set-size effect in a way that is impossible to predict or explain for search processes that iterate over the "set" of items in memory (as though memory is itself just a list of the well-learned items).
text.formatted: People tend to form richer, more distinctive memories for objects of expertise <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Curby et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Ericsson & Lehmann, 1996)</ref>, so if strength dominates, search should be better for the larger, familiar set, reversing the memory set-size effect in a way that is impossible to predict or explain for search processes that iterate over the "set" of items in memory (as though memory is itself just a list of the well-learned items).

text.text: A complication of any such design (including designs that manipulate set size alone) is that memory set size and memory strength cannot be fully unconfounded behaviorally: adding items to a memory list itself tends to weaken the items' representations through interference (the list-length effect; Ratcliff et al., 1990; Shiffrin et al., 1990).
text.formatted: A complication of any such design (including designs that manipulate set size alone) is that memory set size and memory strength cannot be fully unconfounded behaviorally: adding items to a memory list itself tends to weaken the items' representations through interference (the list-length effect; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Ratcliff et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Shiffrin et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while qualitatively we can show a reversal, quantitatively estimating the contributions of memory strength and list length to the decision process requires a proposed model of how the two interact.

For this reason we pair the experiments with simulations of the standard global matching model (REM; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), in which strength and set size are separately specified parameters, alongside response-time extensions of global matching models (Diller et al., 2001; Nosofsky & Palmeri, 1997).
text.formatted: For this reason we pair the experiments with simulations of the standard global matching model (REM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, in which strength and set size are separately specified parameters, alongside response-time extensions of global matching models <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diller et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Nosofsky & Palmeri, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: By calibrating each condition's encoding parameters solely to its observed memory-test performance, the model lets us ask whether a single strength-based mechanism, with no serial search and no parameters fit to the search data, quantitatively accounts for the full pattern of results, and lets us estimate the relative contributions of strength and list length that the data alone cannot fully isolate.
To preview, memory strength reliably improved hybrid search at matched set sizes (Exp. 1) and reversed the set-size effect when pitted against it (Exps.

Drift-diffusion decompositions located the benefit in the quality of memory-match evidence rather than response caution, and the calibrated model reproduced these results along with the canonical set-size cost.
Thus, global matching models on their own, with no search process per se, appear to be sufficient to explain hybrid search's memory components.

To be clear, serial and parallel processing systems are notoriously difficult to distinguish with response-time data (Townsend, 1972 (Townsend, , 1990)), and a serial-scanning model in which the evaluation of each memory item depends on a continuous strength variable could accommodate strength effects (cf. Donkin & Nosofsky, 2012; Moran et al., 2016; Townsend & Fifić, 2004).
text.formatted: To be clear, serial and parallel processing systems are notoriously difficult to distinguish with response-time data <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Townsend, 1972</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Townsend, , 1990))</ref>, and a serial-scanning model in which the evaluation of each memory item depends on a continuous strength variable could accommodate strength effects (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Donkin & Nosofsky, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Moran et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Townsend & Fifić, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Our claim is therefore not that serial memory search is refuted, but that it is unnecessary, as the standard machinery of recognition memory, graded and strength-dependent global matching, well supported by decades of work, suffices to explain hybrid search's memory effects, including the set-size effects that motivated serial scanning accounts, while pure list-length accounts that ignore strength cannot explain the present data.

Experiment 1 tested the basic hypothesis that better-remembered items are searched for more efficiently than weakly remembered items when the memory list is the same size and every item is successfully encoded into memory in both cases.
Participants performed 2 blocks of hybrid search tasks.
In each block, they first remembered a list of 32 items, then searched for the items on that list in a set of visual search displays of varying set sizes.
Memory encoding was systematically varied across two blocks, such that in one block participants saw each item once (shallow-encoding block), as is usually done in hybrid search studies.
In another block, each item was shown 8 times and each time it was seen, participants had to give a short response related to the item to increase memory strength (deep-encoding block).

In both cases, after this initial encoding phase, all objects were tested in a subsequent old/new memory test to ensure they were memorized accurately regardless of block; finally, participants were asked to search for these objects in the hybrid visual search task.

Previous research has shown that pairing encoding tasks with questions that encourage semantic encoding of the stimuli leads to more accurate responses in recognition tasks (Craik, 2002; Craik & Tulving, 1975).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that pairing encoding tasks with questions that encourage semantic encoding of the stimuli leads to more accurate responses in recognition tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Craik, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Craik & Tulving, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: In models of recognition memory, this occurs because more features are encoded more accurately for items that are seen multiple times, making them more discriminable from lures, and deep encoding questions encourage more distinct features to be encoded (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
text.formatted: In models of recognition memory, this occurs because more features are encoded more accurately for items that are seen multiple times, making them more discriminable from lures, and deep encoding questions encourage more distinct features to be encoded <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: In our case, we stacked multiple methods to increase memory strength, as the particular method by which memory strength is increased is not key to our question.

Thus, in this study, the comparison is between a single-exposure condition and a repeated, semantically elaborated condition, so the manipulation is best characterized as a difference in overall memory strength, produced jointly by repetition and depth rather than by depth alone.
We use the labels "deep" and "shallow" for brevity.

We hypothesized that if memory strength affects search independently of the number of items on the list, performance in the hybrid search task would be improved for the deep relative to the shallow encoding condition.
Our final sample consisted of 75 undergraduate students from University of California, San Diego participating for course credit.

A further 16 participants were run and excluded based on the following criteria, chosen in advance: having an overall memory accuracy ≤ 50%, responding outside a 150-10,000 ms window on more than 10% of search trials, or having average search accuracy below 50%.
The final sample had mean age = 19.9 years, range 18-23 (9 male, 64 female, 2 other/undisclosed).
All procedures were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and participants provided informed consent.
Experiments were run online and completed on participants' personal devices.

Sample sizes for all experiments were set in advance at approximately 75 participants after exclusions, providing >95% power to detect within-subject effects of dz ≥ 0.45 at α = .05, and exceeding typical samples in hybrid search studies (e.g., Wolfe, 2012).
text.formatted: Sample sizes for all experiments were set in advance at approximately 75 participants after exclusions, providing >95% power to detect within-subject effects of dz ≥ 0.45 at α = .05, and exceeding typical samples in hybrid search studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The experiment consisted of 2 blocks (1 deep-encoding block, 1 shallow-encoding block) with 3 stages each: encoding, memory test, and visual search (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The experiment consisted of 2 blocks (1 deep-encoding block, 1 shallow-encoding block) with 3 stages each: encoding, memory test, and visual search (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In the encoding stage, participants were shown a set of items that needed to be memorized and subsequently searched for in that block.
The targets were displayed one-at-a-time at the center of the screen for 3 seconds.
In the shallow-encoding condition, each target was shown only once.
In the deepencoding condition, each target was repeated 8 times in a randomized order and followed by a randomly ordered question from a set of 8 related to the item.

The questions were: "What was the object you just saw?", "What is a use for the object you just saw?", "What is another object that looks like the object you just saw?", "What is another object that is related to the object you just saw?", "Where would you normally find this object?", "Where would you normally purchase this object?", "What is an unconventional use for the object you just saw?", "Who would normally use the object you just saw (e.g., architect)?"
Participants were given 1 question per trial and asked to type in a response to the question.
In both conditions, the target set consisted of 32 images selected from the Brady et al. (2008) object set.
text.formatted: In both conditions, the target set consisted of 32 images selected from the <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Brady et al. (2008)</ref> object set.

text.text: The 32 objects in each block were randomly selected from this set for each participant.
In the memory test stage, participants were tested on the items they had studied initially.
Each of the targets and an equal number of random foils were shown one-at-a-time at the center of the screen.
Participants responded with a keypress to indicate whether the item was old or new.
Following each object, participants reported the confidence in their response on a 1 (least confident) to 6 (most confident) scale.
Finally, in the visual search stage, participants searched for the items in the target set.
Items were presented at 128px by 128px, displayed in a jittered manner on an invisible, full-screen 4x4 grid, with random jitter to prevent co-linearity between items.
Each search display contained either 8 (50%) or 16 (50%) objects, with one of the target objects either present (50%) or all target objects absent (50%).
Participants responded with a keypress to indicate whether a target was present or absent.
No search display contained more than a single target.
The experiment consisted of 256 visual search trials (128 per target set).

There were an equal number of target present trials and target absent trials, and an equal number of each visual set size intermixed in both the deep and shallow encoding blocks, and the order of the deep and shallow blocks was counterbalanced across participants.

In the deep encoding condition, participants viewed 32 objects 8 times each in randomized order for 3000ms each, with a question presented after each object (the same question for every object within a pass; e.g., "What is a use for the object you just saw?").
In the shallow encoding condition, a different set of 32 objects were presented only once each for 3000ms without questions, each followed by a self-paced screen to continue.
Objects were drawn from the full image set such that assignment of objects to the deep and shallow sets were random across participants.

Test phase: Participants completed a recognition memory test where they judged whether each presented object was "old" (from the memorized set) or "new" (foil), followed by confidence ratings on a 1-6 scale.
Visual Search phase: Participants searched for any of the memorized objects in displays containing 8 or 16 items, responding whether a target was present or absent.
Each search display contained either one target (50% of trials) or no targets (50% of trials), with response times exceeding 5000ms triggering a faster response prompt.
People remembered the items in both sets well, with near-ceiling confidence, so we could not compute full ROC curves (Brady et al., 2023) and instead report d′ alongside hit and false-alarm rates.
text.formatted: People remembered the items in both sets well, with near-ceiling confidence, so we could not compute full ROC curves <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brady et al., 2023)</ref> and instead report d′ alongside hit and false-alarm rates.

text.text: Memory was reliably stronger in the deepencoding block, d′ = 4.33 (SD = 0.59), than in the shallow-encoding block, d′ = 3.27 (SD = 1.05), t(74) = 8.27, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.95 (hits: .97 vs. .85; false alarms: .02 vs. .05).

5.82 on the 1-6 scale), t(74) = 5.12, p < .001, d = 0.59, as was confidence across all test responses, t(74) = 6.03, p < .001, d = 0.70.

text.text: Thus, although both sets were "in memory" by conventional criteria, the deep-encoding set was represented more strongly.
On each search trial we measured response time and accuracy (Figure 2).
text.formatted: On each search trial we measured response time and accuracy (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Because participants can trade speed for accuracy in visual search (Wolfe, 2018), our planned primary measure was the inverse efficiency score (IES; mean RT divided by proportion correct, per condition cell; Townsend & Ashby, 1983; Bruyer & Brysbaert, 2011), with RT and accuracy also analyzed separately as a secondary analysis.
text.formatted: Because participants can trade speed for accuracy in visual search <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Wolfe, 2018)</ref>, our planned primary measure was the inverse efficiency score (IES; mean RT divided by proportion correct, per condition cell; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Townsend & Ashby, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bruyer & Brysbaert, 2011)</ref>, with RT and accuracy also analyzed separately as a secondary analysis.

text.text: However, because accuracy in some conditions was lower than is ideal for IES, we also report drift-diffusion model fits, which are more robust.

For IES on target-present trials, a 2 (encoding) × 2 (visual set size) repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of visual set size, F(1,74) = 187.47, p < .001, ηp² = .717, a significant effect of encoding, F(1,74) = 11.01, p = .001, ηp² = .130, and no interaction, F(1,74) = 0.80, p = .373, ηp² = .011.

text.text: Target-absent trials showed the same pattern: visual set size, F(1,74) = 410.70, p < .001, ηp² = .847; encoding, F(1,74) = 4.33, p = .041, ηp² = .055; interaction, F(1,74) = 0.59, p = .446, ηp² = .008.

text.text: Search was thus more efficient for the more deeply encoded set at both visual set sizes, on both trial types.
In accuracy, the encoding benefit was robust.

Target-present: visual set size, F(1,74) = 103.62, p < .001, ηp² = .583; encoding, F(1,74) = 31.39, p < .001, ηp² = .298; interaction, F(1,74) = 10.13, p = .002, ηp² = .120 (the encoding benefit was larger at the smaller visual set size).

text.text: Target-absent: visual set size, F(1,74) = 27.07, p < .001, ηp² = .268; encoding, F(1,74) = 35.56, p < .001, ηp² = .325; interaction, F(1,74) = 0.99, p = .323, ηp² = .013.

text.text: In RT, there was no main effect of encoding (target-present: F(1,74) = 1.31, p = .257, ηp² = .017; target-absent: F(1,74) = 1.42, p = .238, ηp² = .019), with significant set-size effects (Fs > 300, ps < .001, ηp² > .80) and small encoding × set size interactions (present: F(1,74) = 6.80, p = .011, ηp² = .084; absent: F(1,74) = 11.83, p < .001, ηp² = .138).

text.text: Although memory was near ceiling, individual items were occasionally missed on the memory pre-test, and such weakly encoded items could in principle be responsible for the search effects.

Restricting target-present trials to targets each participant had correctly endorsed as "old" in the memory test, the encoding effect remained clearly significant in accuracy, F(1,74) = 16.12, p < .001, ηp² = .179, was attenuated in IES, F(1,74) = 3.96, p = .050, ηp² = .051, and was absent in RT (F(1,74) < 0.01, p = .994), as in the full data.

text.text: Some attenuation is expected under a strength account, because excluding memory-test misses removes the lowest-strength items, disproportionately from the shallow condition, restricting the very strength variation under study.
Strength effects nonetheless persist among items that were demonstrably encoded, and the targetabsent benefits, which involve no specific target item, are unaffected by this restriction.

To characterize the encoding effect within a unified speed-accuracy framework that is more robust than IES, we converted each condition cell's accuracy, mean correct RT, and correct-RT variance into the core parameters of a diffusion decision process using EZ-diffusion (Wagenmakers et al., 2007): drift rate (v), boundary separation (a), and non-decision time.
text.formatted: To characterize the encoding effect within a unified speed-accuracy framework that is more robust than IES, we converted each condition cell's accuracy, mean correct RT, and correct-RT variance into the core parameters of a diffusion decision process using EZ-diffusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Wagenmakers et al., 2007)</ref>: drift rate (v), boundary separation (a), and non-decision time.

text.text: If memory strength improves memory-match evidence, it should raise v, the mean rate of evidence accumulation, which in recognition corresponds to the degree of match between the probe and the stored traces (Ratcliff, 1978; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008); if conditions instead differ in how participants trade speed for accuracy, effects should appear in a, the amount of evidence required before a response is initiated.
text.formatted: If memory strength improves memory-match evidence, it should raise v, the mean rate of evidence accumulation, which in recognition corresponds to the degree of match between the probe and the stored traces <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Ratcliff, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008)</ref>; if conditions instead differ in how participants trade speed for accuracy, effects should appear in a, the amount of evidence required before a response is initiated.

text.text: Both halves of this mapping have been validated experimentally: manipulations of stimulus discriminability lower v while accuracy emphasis raises a (Voss et al., 2004), and in recognition memory specifically, studying items twice rather than once raises v with no reliable change in a, while speed-versusaccuracy instructions produce large changes in a (Arnold et al., 2015).

text.text: Note that in this case, this is a measurement model rather than a process model, because display-level search RTs aggregate multiple item evaluations; parameters were therefore estimated separately within each visual set size and trial type, and v should be read as only an effective evidence-quality index per display.

Deep encoding raised drift rates on both target-present trials, F(1,74) = 58.45, p < .001, ηp² = .441, and target-absent trials, F(1,74) = 80.33, p < .001, ηp² = .521, with the size of the drift benefit varying across visual set sizes (encoding × set size interactions: present, F(1,74) = 31.31, p < .001, ηp² = .297; absent, F(1,74) = 10.34, p = .002, ηp² = .123), and with no significant effect on boundary separation (target-present: F(1,74) = 3.59, p = .062, ηp² = .046; target-absent: F(1,74) = 0.01, p = .939).

text.text: Thus, although mean RT showed no encoding effect, the diffusion model recovered a large evidence-quality benefit for the deeply encoded set.
The benefit was expressed in accuracy and RT variability rather than mean speed in this particular experiment.
We found improved hybrid search performance for memory sets encoded more strongly, despite identical list lengths and near-ceiling old/new memory in both conditions.

The benefit appeared in IES on both target-present and target-absent trials, and in this case appeared primarily in accuracy rather than RT; participants searched relatively slowly and carefully overall (mean RT 2.31 s), and speed and accuracy trade off in such tasks (Wolfe, 2018).
text.formatted: The benefit appeared in IES on both target-present and target-absent trials, and in this case appeared primarily in accuracy rather than RT; participants searched relatively slowly and carefully overall (mean RT 2.31 s), and speed and accuracy trade off in such tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Wolfe, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The drift-diffusion decomposition recovered a large evidence-quality benefit even though mean RTs did not differ.

Accounts on which hybrid search performance is determined solely by the number of (sufficiently encoded) items in memory do not predict any difference between these conditions; recognition models predict it directly, as a discriminability difference.
Notably, there are many possible global matching models of recognition memory that make predictions about reaction time.

An effect of memory strength that appears mainly in accuracy is an a priori property of one of these response-time extensions (ARC-REM), in which decision timing reflects an assessment of retrieval completion rather than evidence strength (Diller et al., 2001; Nobel & Shiffrin, 2001;  see Simulation section).
text.formatted: An effect of memory strength that appears mainly in accuracy is an a priori property of one of these response-time extensions (ARC-REM), in which decision timing reflects an assessment of retrieval completion rather than evidence strength <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diller et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nobel & Shiffrin, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> see Simulation section).

text.text: However, given the flexibility with which participants can trade reaction time for accuracy in search tasks, our overall claim rests solely on overall performance integrating the two, rather than any particular reaction time vs. accuracy trade-off.

Experiment 1 demonstrated that memory set size alone isn't sufficient to explain performance on hybrid search tasks and that instead, how well items are encoded in memory is an important factor in supporting hybrid search.
However, the observed performance differences during visual search were driven primarily by differences in accuracy, not response times.

Although this is straightforwardly accounted for by the drift diffusion model that shows drift rates differed with no significant change in boundary separation (i.e., no speed accuracy trade off), it leaves open the possibility that memory strength has some unique effect on just accuracy but not response time.

In addition, as memory set sizes were the same across the deep and shallow encoding conditions, it's unknown if it's possible to make a larger memory set faster to search than a smaller one -which is a key prediction of recognition models that is incompatible with any form of serial memory search through a "list of encoded items" (e.g., that treat all items as present or absent from memory, as in traditional hybrid search proposals).
Thus, in Experiment 2, we aimed to use a stronger memory manipulation.

To accomplish this, we opted to capitalize on items where participants already differ in how quickly and accurately they can encode them, without any training or specific encoding manipulations required on our part: objects of expertise.
People in general form much richer and more distinctive memories for objects of expertise compared to items they are less familiar with (Curby et al., 2009; Ericsson & Lehmann, 1996).
text.formatted: People in general form much richer and more distinctive memories for objects of expertise compared to items they are less familiar with <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Curby et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Ericsson & Lehmann, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, experts extract new and more informative perceptual features than novices, rely on larger and more informative chunks to structure their encoded memories, and select more distinctive information to encode that is more differentiable from other items to avoid interference (Ericsson & Lehmann, 1996).
text.formatted: In particular, experts extract new and more informative perceptual features than novices, rely on larger and more informative chunks to structure their encoded memories, and select more distinctive information to encode that is more differentiable from other items to avoid interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ericsson & Lehmann, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, even if all participants remember the full memory set, experts will in general have richer, stronger and more distinctive memories for objects of their expertise, which should lead to faster hybrid search for such objects.
We recruited self-reported NFL and NHL fans, taking advantage of participants' strong pre-existing knowledge about sports logos.
This allowed us to use the natural variation in the memory representations of sport logos across the two groups at encoding.
Alongside this manipulation of expertise, we also manipulated list length.

We had participants memorize a larger set of logos in their familiar sport and a shorter list in their non-familiar sport-directly testing the hypothesis that memory strength will matter more than this variation in list length per se for hybrid search performance.

In standard hybrid search tasks, larger memory sets will generally be associated with weaker memories because of more interference (e.g., the list length effect, Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), confounding these two possibilities.
text.formatted: In standard hybrid search tasks, larger memory sets will generally be associated with weaker memories because of more interference (e.g., the list length effect, <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, confounding these two possibilities.

text.text: By contrast, in this experiment the two accounts make completely opposite predictions, with list length predicting better performance for the smaller memory set which is less familiar, and memory strength accounts predicting better performance for the larger memory set which is more familiar.

Our final sample comprised 79 participants (mean age = 36.1 years, range 20-74; 63 male, 16 female) recruited via Prolific, where we could pre-screen their sports knowledge to selectively recruit NFL and NHL experts. 26 additional participants were tested and excluded for: any condition cell with an infinite inverse efficiency score, overall search accuracy below 50%, more than 10% of search responses outside the 500-4,500 ms window, or reporting interest in their nominally unfamiliar sport one or more scale points above their nominally familiar sport.
Participants were limited to be U.S. or Canadian-based and compensated at an hourly rate consistent with institutional guidelines.
All procedures were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and participants provided informed consent.
Participants memorized a subset of the possible 32 NFL and 32 NHL logos.

A total of 272 distractor stimuli were used for the memory test foils and the visual search task, consisting of logos of teams from the American Ultimate Disc League (AUDL), logos of teams from various international soccer leagues, and generated logos of similar visual content and quality from VectorStock (http://www.vectorstock.com/).

Participants were assigned to their experimental group -familiar with the NFL or familiar with the NHL -based on their reported familiarity for each league prior to the beginning of the study, using a Prolific pre-screen that allows selecting participants based on their sports' preferences.
All participants then completed 2 blocks of study, test and visual search.
In one block, they were shown and then tested on 12 unfamiliar logos from their non-preferred sport, followed by visual search for those logos.
In the other block, they were shown and tested on 16 familiar logos from their preferred sport, followed by visual search for those logos.

In total there were 32 NHL and 32 NFL logos but only 12 or 16 of them were used as stimuli during memorization for each participant, so they had to remember the particular set of logos they were shown for each sport.
The order of the preferred sport and non-preferred sport blocks were counterbalanced across participants.
In the study phase at the start of each block, participants were instructed to memorize the targets for that memory set.
Targets were shown in random order, one at a time for 3 seconds each, and all targets were shown twice over the course of the presentation to ensure strong encoding even in the non-preferred sport.
Participants then took a recognition test wherein they were presented with either a target or a foil, one at a time, and asked to identify if the logo was one that they just memorized or a new logo.

The number of foils shown in this stage was equal to the number of targets for that block but different for each block as well as different from the distractor stimuli used for the visual search trials.
After each response, participants were asked to rate their confidence in their answer on a scale from 1 to 6.
In the hybrid search stage of the experiment, for each block, participants completed 128 trials of visual search (Figure 3).
