text.text: The familiarity benefit thus reflected better memory-match evidence, not a different speed-accuracy setting.

Overall, we found improved performance in the hybrid search task for memory sets that people were familiar with, and thus represented more strongly in memory, despite having to memorize more objects and thus having a larger memory set size.
In particular, IES was improved for both target-present and target-absent trials for the longer, more familiar lists.
These differences in IES scores reflected benefits in both response times and accuracy.
This is consistent with strengthbased global matching models, in which strongly represented memories produce stronger match signals.
Notably, all of the results clearly go in the direction of better performance for the longer list rather than the shorter list.
A larger memory set did not come with a cost, but instead led to an advantage when that memory set consisted of stronger rather than weaker memories.
No account in which hybrid search performance is a function of memory set size alone can produce this pattern; yet it follows directly from strength-based global matching.

Experiment 2 showed that with a strong enough memory manipulation it is possible to flip the classic memory set size effect, such that a larger memory set is searched more efficiently than a smaller one.
Along with Experiment 1, this suggests that memory set size alone can't explain performance in hybrid search.

However, we considered that in Experiment 2, it is in theory possible for participants to do a category search to find the target rather than specifically look through their memory set (e.g., is there an NFL logo present at all?).

That is because while the memory task focused on ensuring only the subset of NHL or NFL logos were remembered, the visual search trials never included any of the other, non-studied logos from that same sport.

While this did not occur during the memory test -participants in fact rejected new logos better in the longer list of their familiar sport --this introduces the possibility that participants could complete the search task by responding 'present' when any NFL/NHL logo was present instead of responding 'present' when one of the specific logos they encoded for this experiment was present.

Previous literature has demonstrated that search performance can vary depending on whether participants are searching for any objects from a category or a specific target within a category (Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014).
text.formatted: Previous literature has demonstrated that search performance can vary depending on whether participants are searching for any objects from a category or a specific target within a category <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cunningham & Wolfe, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, in Experiment 3, we replicated Experiment 2 but also included lures from the respective sport that weren't in the memorization phase during the visual search, ensuring participants actually searched for the studied logos in particular rather than performing a category search (a strategy the lures render unreliable: responding 'present' to any same-sport logo produces an error on every lure-present target-absent display).

At the same time, lure-present target-absent displays were correctly rejected on 87% of trials, so participants were easily discriminating studied from unstudied logos rather than merely detecting the relevant category.
Lure presence did not significantly affect target-present accuracy (F(1,74) = 3.78, p = .056, ηp² = .049).

Experiment 3 replicated the findings of Experiment 2, with better hybrid search performance for familiar than unfamiliar logos in terms of IES and accuracy on target-present trials and in RT on both trial types.
They also show that the improved hybrid search performance was the result of strongly represented memories and not the product of a simple categorical search for their domain of expertise.
The lure trials also show how the memory decision treats partial matches.
An unstudied logo from the relevant sport is a partial match: it shares category and format features with the studied set while mismatching on item-specific features.
Global matching models predict the observed pattern: partial matches elevate the memory signal, which slows and occasionally defeats rejection.
Graded lure dynamics of this kind are also the data that most strongly constrain models of the underlying decision process (Osth et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Graded lure dynamics of this kind are also the data that most strongly constrain models of the underlying decision process <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Osth et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our central hypothesis is that the results of all three experiments are consistent with what is expected by standard models of recognition memory, in which a probe is compared in parallel to all stored traces and decisions rest on graded match signals, with no item-by-item search through the memory set.
To test this more directly, we simulated all three experiments with REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), the canonical global matching model, and ARC-REM, the reactiontime extension (Diller et al., 2001.
text.formatted: To test this more directly, we simulated all three experiments with REM <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, the canonical global matching model, and ARC-REM, the reactiontime extension <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diller et al., 2001</ref>.

text.text: The simulations aim to establish that no memory "search" is needed to explain hybrid search data, that is, that a single memory strength-based mechanism, with encoding parameters fixed by each condition's memory-test performance and no parameters fit to any search data, reproduces the full pattern, including the set-size effects that motivated serial-scanning accounts and their reversal under our strength manipulations.

While our behavioral experiments 2 and 3 provide strong evidence about the relative contributions of memory strength and list length through the demonstrations that a larger set of familiar items (16 logos) outperformed a smaller set of unfamiliar ones (12 logos), the precise contributions list length alone makes to "weakening" the items still remains unclear, which we examine below in a model where each is an explicit parameter.
In REM, each studied item is stored as a vector of w = 20 arbitrary feature values; each feature is stored with probability S and stored correctly with probability c.
At test, a probe is compared in parallel to every trace, and the average likelihood ratio (the odds, λ) is compared to a criterion, with λ > 1 yielding an "old" response.
text.formatted: At test, a probe is compared in parallel to every trace, and the average likelihood ratio (the odds, λ) is compared to a criterion, with λ > 1 yielding an "old" response.

text.text: A single neutral criterion was used for all conditions, so condition differences come only from encoding.

As in all global matching models, list-length costs arise because each additional trace adds variance to the match signal, not because more items must be examined (Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Shiffrin et al., 1990).
text.formatted: As in all global matching models, list-length costs arise because each additional trace adds variance to the match signal, not because more items must be examined <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark & Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Shiffrin et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than fitting search data, we calibrated each condition's two encoding parameters (S, c) to reproduce that condition's observed memory pre-test d′, constraining the high-strength condition of each experiment to store at least as many and at least as accurate features as its lowstrength counterpart.
For Experiments 2 and 3, which share a design, the calibration targets were the means of the two experiments' memory-test d′ values (treating them as a single experiment for this purpose).
The calibration recovers a sensible mapping of the manipulations onto encoding.

For Experiment 1, shallow encoding was matched at S = 0.50, c = 0.85 and deep encoding gives more features stored more accurately, at S = 0.65, c = 0.90 (giving d′ = 3.32 and 4.63 against observed 3.27 and 4.33).
Thus, deep encoding with eight repetitions can be thought of as storing more, and more accurate, features per item.
All model values reported below come from a single simulation of each condition at its calibrated parameters, run separately from the calibration search.
For Experiments 2-3, the unfamiliar condition led to a match at S = 0.50, c = 0.75 and the familiar condition at S = 0.60, c = 0.75 (giving d′ = 2.93 and 3.26 against targets 2.93 and 3.38).
Thus, expertise can be thought of as resulting in the storage of more features per logo.
Note that the (S, c) solutions are not uniquely identified, one can think of the manipulations as affecting either how much we store or how accurately somewhat interchangeably.
We also note that neighboring combinations fit comparably so parameter interpretations are illustrative rather than exact.
With parameters fixed in this way, REM reproduces every key accuracy-level feature of the data, not just the memory strength it is matched to.
First, at a constant list length of 32 (Experiment 1), stronger encoding produced substantially better per-decision discrimination and a mirror effect (d′ = 4.63 vs.
3.32; hits .99 vs. .94, false alarms .009 vs. .038).

Second, the model reproduces the reversal in Experiments 2-3: per-decision d′ was higher for the larger, stronger set (16 familiar items, d′ = 3.26) than the smaller, weaker one (12 unfamiliar items, d′ = 2.93).

Simulating the unobserved cells of the strength × length crossing shows where this pattern comes from in the model: at matched strength, lengthening the list from 12 to 16 items cost only 0.06-0.15 d′ (unfamiliar strength: 2.93 → 2.87; familiar strength: 3.41 → 3.26), several times smaller than the 0.4-0.5 d′ strength differences from extra memory strength that override it (and far smaller than the 1.3 d′ encoding effect the model produced for Experiment 1).

The two conditions actually tested thus show the observed crossover, with the larger familiar set outperforming the smaller unfamiliar set, even though within either strength level the model's d′ falls slightly as the list lengthens.

Third, with encoding fixed at the weak level and list length varied alone (N = 4-64), the model produces the canonical memory set-size cost in discriminability, with d′ declining approximately log-linearly (3.28, 3.07, 2.83, 2.60, 2.39).
Each doubling of the list length cost a nearly constant 0.21-0.24 d′, as expected if the decline is log-linear.
This is the signature usually attributed to logarithmic serial search, and here it arises purely from match-variance growth.
REM itself is silent about response time, but provides a strength of evidence term that can be turned into reaction time.
Consider the single old/new decision made about one fixated item.

The decision variable is the odds λ that REM computes (e.g., how likely is this to be an old item?), and our manipulations act on this per-decision evidence: stronger encoding raises λ for studied items and, because stronger traces match novel probes more poorly (differentiation; Criss, 2006), lowers it for novel ones, while longer lists add variance to λ for both, making each individual decision less reliable.

text.text: How a change in this evidence surfaces in reaction time behavior then depends on a second, separable assumption about what ends the decision.
In evidence-accumulation extensions, such as the exemplar-based random walk (Nosofsky & Palmeri, 1997), match signals are sampled into an accumulator until a response threshold is reached.
text.formatted: In evidence-accumulation extensions, such as the exemplar-based random walk <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Nosofsky & Palmeri, 1997)</ref>, match signals are sampled into an accumulator until a response threshold is reached.

text.text: A single decision based on better evidence is then both faster and more accurate, and the threshold setting determines the split: cautious, high-threshold settings push accuracy toward ceiling, so strength and list-length effects appear mainly in decision time, whereas speeded, low-threshold settings compress decision times and push the same effects into error rates.

Models of this class, fit to proberecognition data, produce the curvilinear, approximately logarithmic RT set-size functions seen in hybrid search at a visual set size of one (Nosofsky et al., 2014), and they predict that strength should speed decisions, as we observed in Experiments 2-3.
text.formatted: Models of this class, fit to proberecognition data, produce the curvilinear, approximately logarithmic RT set-size functions seen in hybrid search at a visual set size of one <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Nosofsky et al., 2014)</ref>, and they predict that strength should speed decisions, as we observed in Experiments 2-3.

text.text: In retrieval-completion extensions (ARC-REM; Diller et al., 2001), the decision instead ends when a fixed proportion of probe features has been processed.
text.formatted: In retrieval-completion extensions (ARC-REM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Diller et al., 2001)</ref>, the decision instead ends when a fixed proportion of probe features has been processed.

text.text: A single decision's duration is then set by retrieval dynamics rather than by the evidence, so strength and list length leave decision time nearly untouched and their effects fall entirely on accuracy, whatever its level.

This limiting case was motivated by data in which encoding manipulations moved accuracy but not latency (Nobel & Shiffrin, 2001), and it is the natural account of Experiment 1, where the encoding benefit appeared in accuracy with flat mean RTs even though accuracy was well below ceiling.
text.formatted: This limiting case was motivated by data in which encoding manipulations moved accuracy but not latency <ref type="bibr">(Nobel & Shiffrin, 2001)</ref>, and it is the natural account of Experiment 1, where the encoding benefit appeared in accuracy with flat mean RTs even though accuracy was well below ceiling.

text.text: To verify this prediction, which runs counter to the intuition that stronger evidence should affect both reaction time and accuracy, we implemented ARC-REM with encoding parameters calibrated the same way: it reproduced the same d′ patterns while producing nearly identical per-decision retrieval times across strength conditions (within 5% of each other; e.g., per-decision times of roughly 1.40 vs.
1.47 s for shallow vs. deep hits in Experiment 1, despite the 0.9 d′ accuracy difference between them).foot_2 Which of these extensions better describes a given task plausibly depends on its pacing.

text.text: The drift-diffusion model fits reported with each experiment provide an empirical estimate of this per-decision evidence quality, and in all three experiments, strength raised target-present drift rates while response caution was unchanged.

Finally, to show how such a model can produce display-level hybrid search effects, we embedded it in a minimal hybrid search wrapper motivated by the eye-tracking finding that observers perform one memory check per fixated item (Drew et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Finally, to show how such a model can produce display-level hybrid search effects, we embedded it in a minimal hybrid search wrapper motivated by the eye-tracking finding that observers perform one memory check per fixated item <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Drew et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Although this is a naive model of search, it provides some guidance.

In it, display items are processed in random order, each receiving one model decision (drawn from the ARC-REM extension, which supplies per-decision times), terminating at the first "old" response (with a stricter criterion than single-probe recognition as appropriate when false alarms compound over multiple display items; Chun & Wolfe, 1996).
text.formatted: In it, display items are processed in random order, each receiving one model decision (drawn from the ARC-REM extension, which supplies per-decision times), terminating at the first "old" response (with a stricter criterion than single-probe recognition as appropriate when false alarms compound over multiple display items; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chun & Wolfe, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: This simple model reproduces the display-level structure of the empirical results.

Response times rise steeply with visual set size for present and absent trials, and search accuracy and target-absent efficiency are better for the strong memory set at both visual set sizes in both experimental designs, including better performance for the 16-item familiar set than for the 12item unfamiliar set.

For example, at the largest display sizes, the model's target-present accuracy was .96 for the deep vs. .91 for the shallow set (Experiment 1) and .91 for the familiar vs. .83 for the unfamiliar set (Experiments 2-3), and its target-absent inverse efficiency favored the strong sets by 7% and 10%, respectively.
Target-absent inverse efficiency doubled from the smaller to the larger displays in every condition, mirroring the steep visual set-size slopes in the data.

Thus, the memory set-size effects that motivated serial-scanning accounts of hybrid search are fully consistent with, and straightforwardly explained by, the same strength-based matching process that explains recognition memory at large.

Hybrid search performance has canonically been understood in terms of how many items must be processed, both in the visual search through the display and in the memory search through the target set, with the logarithmic memory set-size cost attributed to an efficient serial search through the memorized list (Wolfe, 2012).

text.text: A hybrid search display is, on this view, a recognition test with multiple simultaneous probes, effectively list recognition with many "new" items per test (cf. Wixted et al., 2021).

text.text: We have deliberately framed our conclusion in terms of the sufficiency of standard global matching models, rather than suggesting no serial model could ever account for the data.

Serial and parallel architectures can mimic one another closely in response-time data (Townsend, 1972 (Townsend, , 1990)), distinguishing them requires distributional or factorial methods purpose-built for the question (Donkin & Nosofsky, 2012; Moran et al., 2016; Townsend & Fifić, 2004; Townsend & Nozawa, 1995), and a serial-scanning model in which each item's evaluation depends on a continuous strength variable could likely accommodate strength effects on search.
text.formatted: Serial and parallel architectures can mimic one another closely in response-time data <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Townsend, 1972</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Townsend, , 1990))</ref>, distinguishing them requires distributional or factorial methods purpose-built for the question <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Donkin & Nosofsky, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Moran et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Townsend & Fifić, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Townsend & Nozawa, 1995)</ref>, and a serial-scanning model in which each item's evaluation depends on a continuous strength variable could likely accommodate strength effects on search.

text.text: The present data do rule out any account on which hybrid search performance is determined by the number of well-encoded items in memory, with items treated as interchangeable list entries.
Such accounts cannot produce better performance for a longer list.

Our positive claim is based on parsimony, that is, the strength-based global matching machinery independently required to explain recognition memory, and well established over decades of recognition memory research, can explain hybrid search's memory effects as well.
It even predicts the logarithmic set-size cost that motivated serial-scanning interpretations, so no additional serial search mechanism need be posited.

Distinguishing serial from parallel architectures directly would require designs borrowed from systems-factorial tests, or analyses of how lure processing changes with memory set size (Moran et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Distinguishing serial from parallel architectures directly would require designs borrowed from systems-factorial tests, or analyses of how lure processing changes with memory set size <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Moran et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Experiment 3's lure trials already exhibit the basic phenomenon such analyses would exploit, where categorically related, unstudied items reliably slow rejection and elevate false alarms.

Crossing such lures with memory set size and parametrically varied repetition (to map a quantitative strength dimension; cf. Hockley, 1982) is, in our view, the most promising route to architectural tests in hybrid search if positive evidence is to be found for a "memory search" account beyond global matching models.
text.formatted: Crossing such lures with memory set size and parametrically varied repetition (to map a quantitative strength dimension; cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hockley, 1982)</ref> is, in our view, the most promising route to architectural tests in hybrid search if positive evidence is to be found for a "memory search" account beyond global matching models.

text.text: Our results should not be read as showing that memory set size is irrelevant; in the model, and likely in behavior, both factors operate on the same match signal.

Indeed, because adding items to memory weakens each item's representation through interference, set-size manipulations are usually also -at least in part -strength manipulations (Ratcliff et al., 1990; Shiffrin et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Indeed, because adding items to memory weakens each item's representation through interference, set-size manipulations are usually also -at least in part -strength manipulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Ratcliff et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Shiffrin et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: This is why the two cannot be fully unconfounded behaviorally, and why modeling is required to separate them.

Our calibrated REM model quantifies this for our designs: over the 12-to-16-item range, the pure list-length cost is small (0.06-0.15 d′) relative to the strength differences our manipulations produced (0.4-0.5 d′ in Experiments 2-3, and 1.3 d′ in Experiment 1, against an observed memory test difference of 1.06 d′), which is why the reversal occurs.

With much larger set-size ranges (e.g., 4 to 100; Wolfe, 2012), list-length costs will be substantial, driving memory strength way down, unless strength manipulations between list lengths are correspondingly large.
text.formatted: With much larger set-size ranges (e.g., 4 to 100; <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wolfe, 2012)</ref>, list-length costs will be substantial, driving memory strength way down, unless strength manipulations between list lengths are correspondingly large.

text.text: Thus, we argue that hybrid search efficiency reflects the discriminability of memory-match signals, to which both the number and the strength of stored representations contribute.

This view is consonant with the broader recognition literature, where even the existence of pure list-length effects is contested once strength-related confounds are controlled (Dennis et al., 2008; Kinnell & Dennis, 2011; Osth & Dennis, 2015).
text.formatted: This view is consonant with the broader recognition literature, where even the existence of pure list-length effects is contested once strength-related confounds are controlled <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dennis et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kinnell & Dennis, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Osth & Dennis, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It is likely the case in hybrid search as well that list length effects independent of strength will be small or hard to provide direct evidence for, but this is currently a model-based conclusion rather than something we have directly tested.
Work on memory-set partitioning has already begun to map the limits on how observers can engage the items held in memory.

Observers generally cannot restrict search to an arbitrary relevant subset of memorized items (Boettcher et al., 2018), but can when subsets are categorically distinct (Gronau et al., 2024), and display properties can guide which memories are interrogated (Nordfang & Wolfe, 2018).
text.formatted: Observers generally cannot restrict search to an arbitrary relevant subset of memorized items <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Boettcher et al., 2018)</ref>, but can when subsets are categorically distinct <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gronau et al., 2024)</ref>, and display properties can guide which memories are interrogated <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Nordfang & Wolfe, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The original authors interpreted these phenomena through a guided-search lens, as a serial memory search limited to context-relevant items.

However, they are equally natural under global matching, since memory traces include context features, so context-congruent traces produce stronger match signals and dominate the decision (Clark & Gronlund, 1996), with graded rather than all-or-none selection.
text.formatted: However, they are equally natural under global matching, since memory traces include context features, so context-congruent traces produce stronger match signals and dominate the decision <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark & Gronlund, 1996)</ref>, with graded rather than all-or-none selection.

text.text: Our strength effects are complementary, in that partitioning work shows that which memories are most affecting search depends on structure and context match, and we show that how strongly each memory matches governs efficiency even within a fixed set.
There are likely constraints on the generality of the findings we present here.
For example, the present findings are based on adult participants tested in controlled laboratory and online settings using simplified visual displays and well-defined target sets.

Although these tasks were designed to capture core properties of everyday hybrid search, real-world searches like those performed in airport security screening, medical image interpretation, or educational assessment often involve more complex stimuli, higher stakes, and extended training histories.

As a result, while our results suggest that strengthening memory representations may improve search performance in such applied domains, future work will be necessary to directly test whether the same mechanisms operate under those conditions.
Our strength manipulations also covaried with stimulus class differences across experiments (everyday objects vs. logos) and, in Experiments 2-3, with participants' broader domain knowledge.

The model's calibration absorbs such differences into its encoding parameters, but which aspects of expertise produce stronger logo memories (perceptual experience, semantic knowledge, affective engagement) is a question for future work.

Finally, each of our experiments included only two visual set sizes, and thus we cannot directly measure whether visual set size affected performance linearly, as expected based on previous work; further work, especially with larger visual set-size ranges, is needed to clarify how the functional form of RT increases in hybrid search relate to combined models of visual search and recognition memory (Wixted et al., 2021).

text.text: Memory strength matters to hybrid search, independently of memory set size, and strength manipulations can outweigh and even reverse set-size effects.

A standard global matching model of recognition memory, calibrated only to memory-test performance, captures these results together with the canonical set-size costs that originally motivated serial-search accounts.

Models of recognition memory thus provide a productive, mechanistic framework for the memory component of hybrid visual search; integrating them with models of visual attention is the natural next step toward a full account of hybrid search.
Figure 1.
Experimental procedure for Experiment 1.
The experiment consisted of three phases with two different encoding conditions.

Memorization phase: In the deep encoding condition, participants viewed 32 objects 8 times each in randomized order for 3000ms each, with a question presented after each object (the same question for every object within a pass; e.g., "What is a use for the object you just saw?").
In the shallow encoding condition, a different set of 32 objects were presented only once each for 3000ms without questions, each followed by a self-paced screen to continue.
Objects were drawn from the full image set such that assignment of objects to the deep and shallow sets were random across participants.

Test phase: Participants completed a recognition memory test where they judged whether each presented object was "old" (from the memorized set) or "new" (foil), followed by confidence ratings on a 1-6 scale.
Visual Search phase: Participants searched for any of the memorized objects in displays containing 8 or 16 items, responding whether a target was present or absent.
Each search display contained either one target (50% of trials) or no targets (50% of trials), with response times exceeding 5000ms triggering a faster response prompt.

In sum, the standard global matching model, calibrated only to memory-test performance, produces (a) the classic, approximately log-linear memory set-size cost in discriminability; (b) strength benefits at equal list length; and (c) the reversal of the set-size effect when the longer list is more strongly encoded.
The response-time extensions of global matching show that these benefits can appear in accuracy, in speed, or in both, depending on what ends each decision.
not built to answer: what happens when the items are all in memory, but differ in how strongly they are represented?
Across three experiments, memory strength had large effects on hybrid search efficiency -independently of list length.

Strengthening memories through repetition and elaborative encoding improved search at a fixed memory set size (Exp. 1); and when strength was pitted against list length using sports-logo expertise, participants searched a 16-item familiar set faster and more accurately than a 12-item unfamiliar set, reversing the canonical memory setsize effect (Exps.
The reversal held even with within-category lures that precluded categorical search strategies (Exp.

A global matching recognition model calibrated only to each condition's memory-test performance reproduced the full pattern, including the approximately log-linear set-size cost in discriminability itself, with no search process going through memory, just evidence variability and match signals.
The expression of the strength benefit differed across experiments, being primarily accuracy in Experiment 1, and both accuracy and RT in Experiments 2-3.
The drift-diffusion fits reported in each experiment suggest that this variability reflects a single underlying effect.
In all three experiments, memory strength raised target-present drift rates (the quality of memorymatch evidence) while leaving response caution unchanged.
How that improved evidence expresses itself then depends on what times the decision, and participants may have timed their decisions differently in the two kinds of task.

In Experiment 1, where search responses were slower each memory check could run to retrieval completion, and under retrieval-completion timing (ARC-REM) strength effects fall on accuracy even when accuracy is well below ceiling, which is what we observed.

Experiments 2-3, with their faster search responses, are closer to the setting where threshold-based accumulation (EBRW) is often applied, and strength there produced the predicted joint benefits to speed and accuracy.
The cross-experiment differences may therefore not be only noise but may reflect the expected behavior of strength-based mechanisms under different decision-timing scenarios.
